items.title: Random matrix discrepancy -- CLuP algorithm and parametric RDT approach
items.summary: We study information-theoretic and algorithmic aspects of random matrix discrepancy in proportional regime. The problem amounts to finding $\kappa=\min_{\x\in\mB^n}\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bar{A}_i\x_i\|_2$, where $\bar{A}_i\in\mR^{d\times d}$ is a collection of $n$ iid GOE matrices, $\mB^n$ are vertices of the unit cube in $\mR^n$, and $\alpha=\lim_{n\rightarrow \infty}\frac{n}{d^2}$ is a proportionality constant. Strong progress is made in several directions: (i) We develop a Random duality theory (RDT) framework and utilize its a lifted variant to establish lower bounds on $\kappa$, which precisely match the bounds obtained via the first moment in [81]. (ii) To address analytical challenges, we propose a negative Hopfield model as a proxy for implementation of a fully lifted RDT. On the 2nd lifting level, this model fits remarkably well between the information-theoretic lower bounds from [81] and the algorithmic upper bounds from [38]. (iii) On the 3rd and 4th lifting levels, parametric RDT concepts predict a sizeable computational gap for lower $\kappa$ values in the proxy model. Extending proxy information-theoretic fitting to algorithmic suggests a similar computational gap for matrix discrepancy in low $\kappa$ regime, aligning with [73]. (iv) We design a Controlled Loosening Up (CLuP) algorithm for matrix discrepancy. Its performance strongly matches our analytical results -- closely approaching information-theoretic predictions in lower $\alpha$ ranges (indicating a small or nonexistent computational gap) and following the proxy model's algorithmic predictions in higher $\alpha$ ranges (indicating a sizeable computational gap). Both the information-theoretic and algorithmic predictions match the corresponding phenomenologies of the symmetric binary perceptron (SBP) vector analogue in the entire $\alpha\in(0,\infty)$ range [1,2,14,31,51,92,111].

items.title: MagBerry: A Julia package for modeling magnon and phonon topology and transport
items.summary: We present MagBerry, a Julia package for studying the topology and transport of magnons, phonons, and their hybrid excitations. It combines magnetic models and linear spin-wave Hamiltonians from Sunny.jl with native modules for harmonic phonons and magnon--phonon coupling. These excitations are treated within a common bosonic Bogoliubov--de Gennes formulation. The package calculates bulk and boundary spectra, Berry curvature, and Chern numbers, and resolves the spin and phonon angular momentum carried by each mode. Transport calculations include thermal Hall, spin and orbital Nernst, and phonon angular momentum Hall responses. The package also evaluates the extended Berry curvature dipole contribution to nonlinear magnon thermal Hall transport. Relaxation-time Boltzmann theory gives heat and angular momentum currents. Examples based on published models reproduce topological magnon boundary spectra and illustrate phonon geometry and nonlinear transport. For an altermagnetic hybrid model, we extend a published study of the d-wave phonon angular momentum texture by calculating its Boltzmann transport coefficients. The resulting tensor describes how the longitudinal and transverse angular momentum currents vary with temperature and the direction of the temperature gradient.

items.title: Liquid-liquid criticality in a fluid whose two structures favor mixing
items.summary: The generic two-state description of liquid polyamorphism requires a non-ideality opposing mixing for liquid-liquid separation. This condition assumes that the free energy of the underlying fluid is independent of the structural order, an assumption that fails when the local structures differ in size or attraction. We derive a closed-form stability condition after density relaxation for a van der Waals closure based on the second virial coefficient of a pair potential whose internal state determines both the contact distance and the well depth. The condition recovers the familiar result for structures identical in size and attraction but can change sign within the liquid when they differ. In ten of the thirty-four parameter sets examined, a critical state preferred by the liquid requires a non-ideality favoring mixing. For one such fluid, we construct the coexistence curve, which terminates at the predicted critical point at positive pressure. Attraction and excluded volume provide distinct contributions to the density-order coupling; only the former survives on a fixed lattice with single occupancy. Removing the excluded-volume contribution restores the familiar condition in 58 of the 82 such critical states found. Thus, within this closure, liquid-liquid separation can occur with a non-ideality favoring mixing.

items.title: Magnon binding in a quantum Hall ferromagnet with a periodic electric field
items.summary: A spin wave in a filling-one quantum Hall ferromagnet is neutral but carries an electric dipole perpendicular to its momentum. A spatially periodic electrostatic potential therefore creates parallel channels for spin waves. We use this established mechanism to calculate how confinement changes the exchange binding of magnons travelling in the same direction. Narrower channels increase the overlap of their transverse wavefunctions and strengthen the effective attraction. In an isolated harmonic channel, the energy required to remove one magnon from a cluster of $N$ is $\pi(k_*\ell)^4N(N-1)/4$ times the transverse level spacing to leading order, where $k_*$ is the mean wave number along the channel and $\ell$ is the magnetic length. We predict the frequency and momentum dependence of the spectral line for adding a second magnon to one already present, both in an isolated channel and in a coupled array. Tunnelling in a wide array can make the binding energy exponentially small, while a strip narrower than the transverse pair size recovers one-dimensional binding at sufficiently weak attraction. We also find that a moving potential can carry a single wave packet with less spreading than free propagation when its initial group velocity matches the potential's speed.

items.title: Lower Bound of Thermal Conductivity in Graphene
authors: Yan Gao, Yafei Ding, Hongbin Xu, Zhaoxuan Tang, Fuqing Duan, Wenmei Luo, Zhensheng Zhang, Xiaohang Zhang, Guimei Zhu, Yahui Xue, Baowen Li
items.summary: The intrinsic thermal conductivity ($\kappa$) of graphene remains highly controversial because of physical and metrological complexities. Although the thermal bridge method enables reliable measurements, sample fabrication remains challenging. Here, we develop a highly efficient patterning and transfer technique to systematically fabricate and characterize suspended bilayer graphene (BLG) thermal bridges with lengths of 1-30 $\mu$m. Suspended BLG with unavoidable polymer residues exhibits length-independent thermal conductivity of approximately 570 W/(m K) at room temperature, remaining nearly constant from 250 to 350 K and robust to rigorous surface cleaning and amorphous silicon nitride substrates. Homogeneous non-equilibrium molecular dynamics (HNEMD) simulations show that amorphous carbon coverage of only approximately 0.01 monolayer is sufficient to suppress out-of-plane flexural acoustic (ZA) phonons. These findings challenge the prevailing view that rigid substrates suppress ZA phonons more strongly than surface contamination and identify a robust lower bound of $\kappa$ governed by amorphous surface scattering. This lower bound reflects heat conduction in graphene under realistic device conditions and provides a reference for fundamental phonon transport studies and the integration of graphene into thermal management applications in electronic devices and chips.

items.title: A Practitioner's Guide to Materials Theory and Computation in the Age of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence
items.summary: Computational modelling has become a cornerstone of materials science, with advances in atomistic simulations, high-throughput computation, and artificial intelligence transforming how materials are understood, discovered, and designed. These developments build upon generations of theoretical innovations that have translated complex mathematical and physical principles into practical predictive tools. However, the growing diversity of computational methods presents challenges for practitioners seeking a coherent understanding of their theoretical foundations. Drawing upon the author's research experience, this monograph provides a practitioner-oriented, pedagogical overview of computational materials science, unified through the concepts of potential-energy landscapes and statistical sampling. It explores how these concepts underpin structural stability, phase behaviour, and electronic and magnetic properties, through a systematic treatment of empirical force fields, density-functional theory, many-body electronic-structure methods, statistical sampling, and property prediction. It further examines high-throughput workflows, materials databases, and the probabilistic foundations of artificial intelligence. Particular emphasis is placed on atomistic representations, graph neural networks, and generative models, highlighting the roles of symmetry, group theory, differential geometry, and stochastic processes in modern materials modelling. By connecting established physical theories with emerging data-driven approaches, this monograph offers a unified perspective on computational materials science and identifies opportunities and challenges toward physics-informed, efficient, and reliable materials discovery.

items.title: Interaction between fluids and Helfrich membranes
authors: Dennis W\"orthm\"uller, Pierre Sens, Michele Castellana
items.summary: We propose a finite-element method to determine the dynamics of a fluid interacting with a membrane---a fluid layer equipped with a Helfrich elastic free energy [W. Helfrich, Z. Naturforschung C, 28, 693, (1973)]. Our analysis is based on a partitioned approach, where the state of the fluid, of the membrane, and of the mesh, are solved for at staggered steps. We show the predicting capabilities of the method by considering a macroscopic example of an elastomer membrane, which bulges as it interacts with air injected through a channel. We demonstrate that our method allows for describing large membrane deformations which are not accessible by perturbative methods. We discuss the limitations of our method, by characterizing its added-mass instability. Finally, we show how our analysis allows for understanding the physical mechanism of bulge formation, which is due to a combination of elastic stresses and membrane boundary conditions.

items.title: Quantum Cooling by Classical Shadows
items.summary: Cooling to ground states of many-body Hamiltonians by imaginary-time evolution is central to quantum simulation, but its non-unitary aspect prevents direct implementation on a quantum computer. Existing routes restore it by importing structure from outside the intrinsic quantum dynamics, e.g. by parameter estimation on many copies or recursive compilation. Here, we show that a single randomized snapshot of the quantum many-body system is sufficient to steer the state along the cooling direction on average. Our algorithm, shadow chain, uses randomized measurements to collapse the state to its classical record, which fixes the next unitary update. Snapshots across steps form a trajectory that is a quantum-executable sample of an auxiliary-field path integral; fluctuations among trajectories are exponentially suppressed in system size. With the randomness supplied intrinsically by the Born measurement rule, the trajectories sample themselves rather than going through external accept-reject steps. The resulting algorithm is ansatz-free and exact upon extrapolation to the continuous limit, with the exponential cost confined only to system size rather than temperature.

items.title: Gapless Nature of Spin Liquid in the $S=1/2$ Kagome Heisenberg Antiferromagnet with Neural-Network Quantum States
authors: Andreas Raikos, Alessandro Sinibaldi, Riccardo Rende, Giuseppe Carleo, Federico Becca, Luciano Loris Viteritti
items.summary: Whether the spin-$1/2$ kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet hosts a gapped $\mathbb{Z}_2$ or a gapless $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid remains a central open question in frustrated magnetism. Here, we address this question by directly computing the triplet gap with a neural-network quantum state that does not presuppose any specific spin-liquid structure. Applying a time-reversal symmetric transformer-based ansatz to clusters of up to $768$ sites, we obtain state-of-the-art variational energies on two-dimensional lattices with periodic boundary conditions and estimate an energy per site of $-0.43873(12)$ in the thermodynamic limit. Finite-size scaling of the magnetic order parameter and triplet excitation gap shows that both extrapolate to zero in the thermodynamic limit. Together, these results provide independent and direct evidence of a gapless spin-liquid ground state, consistent with the $U(1)$ Dirac spin liquid. More broadly, they demonstrate that neural-network quantum states can resolve ground-state properties of frustrated quantum magnets that remain challenging for conventional numerical methods.

items.title: Flexible ground-state search algorithm on hybrid Clifford-tensor network manifolds
authors: Hari Timsina, Antonio Francesco Mello, Meghadeepa Adhikary, Marcello Dalmonte, Mario Collura
items.summary: Tensor network algorithms face challenges in highly entangled regimes, such as systems with periodic boundary conditions (PBC), long-range interactions, or higher dimensions, where the required bond dimension quickly renders computations infeasible. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel approach that integrates the stabilizer formalism directly into the traditional density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithm. While previous methods have used Clifford unitaries to minimize ground-state entanglement, fundamentally limited to distilling that away utilizing local two-qubit operations, our framework optimizes Clifford transformations to minimize the state's energy. We benchmark our method against standard DMRG at fixed bond dimensions for the Ising model on a ring (including long-range interactions) and on a torus. We observe systematic gains in models with local interactions - as drastic as a factor of 40 decrease in bond dimension in two dimensions. Our algorithm is readily implementable in standard DMRG codes and provides a practical way to substantially reduce algorithm costs, paving the way for large-scale simulation at volumes beyond what is presently achievable.

items.title: Coupling-Response Thermodynamic Density of States for Bosonic Working Media
authors: Francisco J. Pe\~na, Bastian Castorene, Nicolas Vidal-Silva
items.summary: We introduce an operational thermodynamic density of states (TDOS), $\mathcal{G}_\lambda=(\partial S/\partial\lambda)_{T,\mu}$, to characterize bosonic working media under microscopic spectral control. At fixed chemical potential, the response is strictly driven by the structural density of states, yielding the exact scaling law $\mathcal{G}_\lambda=-(d/\alpha)S/\lambda$ for homogeneous spectra $\epsilon(k)=\Delta+\lambda k^\alpha$, while coupling-dependent gaps generate edge terms only for finite boundary weight. Under a fixed-particle constraint, a secondary chemical-potential redistribution channel emerges. Exact solutions for quadratic bands and harmonic traps demonstrate that spatial dimensionality dictates whether this constrained TDOS exhibits a jump discontinuity or remains continuous across the Bose--Einstein condensation threshold. For pure scale control, the response maps exactly to the heat capacity, $\lambda \mathcal{G}_\lambda^{(N)}=-C_N$. This framework is applied to evaluate reversible work in Stirling cycles and to identify observables in magnonic platforms, contrasting global spectral edges with topological Dirac gaps in honeycomb ferromagnets.

items.title: Predictive sufficiency as an information microscope for time-resolved coherent scattering
authors: Christian Gutt, Amir Tosson, Nimmi Das Anthuparambil, Jovita Lukasik, Michael M\"oller
items.summary: X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) measures dynamics through the evolution of coherent speckle patterns, most commonly summarized by intensity correlation functions. These averages describe relaxation but can conceal how speckle fluctuations evolve in time and across reciprocal space. Here we introduce an information microscope that tests whether a chosen set of XPCS observables retains the information needed to describe subsequent measured scattering dynamics. A learned representation of the present speckle sequence indicates when information remains outside the chosen description; an XPCS Alphabet then searches for experimentally accessible observables that recover it. In simulated Bragg scattering, speckle activity and anisotropy reveal signatures of correlated deformation and intermittent slip. In a controlled SAXS model, fluctuations of speckle activity provide sensitivity to the spatial extent of cooperative particle motion. In a two-dimensional glass former, retaining time-resolved speckle correlations and radial intensity recovers information lost in the average relaxation function. The fluctuations of these correlations become stronger during caging, without selecting a single dominant correlated mode. This approach uses learning to guide the physical analysis of coherent scattering, while keeping the resulting XPCS observables measurable and interpretable.

items.title: Measurement of Magnonic Quantum Geometry
authors: S. Kim, M. Stone, S. E. Nagler, A. D. Christianson, Jiabin Yu, S. Okamoto, H. Miao
items.summary: Quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in macroscopic quantum phenomena, including quantum Hall effects and flat-band superconductivity. However, since quantum geometry is encoded in wavefunctions rather than energy spectra, direct experimental characterization remains a formidable challenge. This challenge is particularly acute for quasiparticles in quantum materials, whose wavefunctions are generally inferred from effective low-energy models rather than measured directly. Here, we establish an experimental framework for characterizing the quantum geometry of magnons, a ubiquitous Bosonic quasiparticle of magnetically ordered states. We show that the inelastic neutron scattering (INS) cross-section measures geometric parameters of the spinor wavefunctions of ferromagnets. By tracking the energy- and momentum-dependent INS intensity, we extract the quantum geometric tensor without requiring detailed knowledge of microscopic spin-spin interactions. Our results establish magnons as an ideal arena for experimentally probing quantum geometry and open new avenues for exploring geometry-driven magnon transport and quantum Fisher information in magnetic materials.

items.title: On-demand valley control in a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure via optically programmed magnetic order
authors: Muhammad Hassan Shaikh, Daria Blach, Harishankar Jayakumar, Brayan Eraso Solarte, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Yafei Ren, Archana Raja, Chitraleema Chakraborty
items.summary: The ability to optically control the valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional semiconductors is critical for scalable valleytronics. While magnetic proximity effects can lift valley degeneracy, static interfaces lack the dynamic control needed for devices. Here, we demonstrate on-demand optical switching of valley symmetry breaking in a WSe2/CrPS4 heterostructure by exploiting light-tunable magnetic order. Using polarization- and time-resolved photoluminescence, we show that excitation below the ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) gap preserves an out-of-plane N\'eel vector in CrPS4, generating a net out-of-plane spin at the interface and enabling spin-polarized charge transfer. This yields a robust polarization gap in the WSe2 A-exciton decay dynamics without an external magnetic field. Excitation above the LMCT gap extinguishes the polarization gap, indicating a rotation of the N\'eel vector to in-plane. This reversible switching provides direct evidence of spin-polarized charge transfer. Furthermore, the same optical excitation enables optical control of the decay dynamics of the low-energy excitons (XLE) by ~42%, which is potentially attributed to the modification of interfacial couplings. Our work establishes a first unique multifunctional platform where magnetic symmetry, valley polarization, and exciton relaxation are integrated and dynamically controlled by light.

items.title: From RuP$_3$SiO$_{11}$ to Ideal Geometry: Parallel-Face Octahedra for Kitaev-Dominated Interactions
authors: Do Hoon Kiem, Satoshi Okamoto, Tom Berlijn
items.summary: RuP$_3$SiO$_{11}$ has recently been identified as a Kitaev spin liquid candidate via neutron scattering. To assess its proximity to the Kitaev limit, we perform \textit{ab initio} calculations of magnetic interactions, finding good agreement for the Kitaev and off-diagonal exchanges, while the Heisenberg exchange is ferromagnetic rather than the experimentally fitted antiferromagnetic one. We also identify a sizable antiferromagnetic out-of-plane exchange not captured in previous analyses. Extending the study to eight substitutional analogs in the $MT_3Q$O$_{11}$ family ($M$ = Ru, Os; $T$ = P, As; $Q$= Si, Ge), we observe strong variations in magnetic interactions, highlighting the tunability of this materials class. Finally, inspired by RuP$_3$SiO$_{11}$, which exhibits a near parallel-face octahedral arrangement, we compare idealized geometries and show that the parallel-face configuration yields a Kitaev-dominated regime, suggesting a new structural route to the Kitaev limit.

items.title: Nonlinear spin generation and spin photocurrent as a symmetry and magnetic domain probe in unconventional magnets
authors: Ying Xiong, Er-Ping Li, L. K. Ang
items.summary: Unconventional magnets host momentum-dependent spin splitting without spin-orbit coupling. We demonstrate that the combination of nonlinear spin polarisation and spin photocurrent is a powerful diagnostic tool for probing the spin space group symmetry, magnetic domain, and quantum geometry in unconventional magnets, providing information beyond their equilibrium spin texture. We develop a mechanism-resolved joint symmetry analysis of second-order spin photoresponse tensors and analyse their frequency dependence, magnetic parity and relaxation scaling. We show that unconventional magnets are natural platforms to achieve large magnetic-even spin photocurrent induced by unpolarised light, making them promising candidates for polariser-free spin sources. We present numerical illustrations for prototypical hybrid parity and odd parity magnet models. Our work provides optical fingerprints connecting spin-space symmetry to distinct microscopic pathways of spin accumulation and transport.

items.title: Beyond global density in a stochastic sandpile: the role of spatial signatures in the predictability of extremes
authors: Kamil P. Orzechowski, Julian Sienkiewicz, Piotr Fronczak
items.summary: In self-organized critical systems the global load is a strong precursor of extreme events. In the two-dimensional Manna sandpile, grain density alone predicts extreme avalanches with an AUC of about 0.96. We ask whether density fully determines the system's readiness for an extreme event, that is, whether microstates with the same number of grains are equivalent. Because density is such a strong predictor, a method that sees the full microstate can score well just by counting grains. We therefore compare only states with an identical number of grains. Even then, both a parameter-free statistic and a convolutional network distinguish states that precede an extreme avalanche from typical ones, while shuffled controls do not. The signal is a load contrast between the center and the dissipative boundaries, carried by the two lowest symmetric cosine modes. Their normalized energy is a single variable that needs no training. Together with density it recovers most of the gain that a network trained on the full microstate achieves over density alone. Readiness for an extreme avalanche therefore depends both on the total load and on how that load is distributed relative to the boundaries.

items.title: Finite-time quenches across first-, second-, and infinite-order transitions in XXZ spin chains
authors: Luiz Felipe Santos Dittberner, Luigi Berber, Maria C. O. Aguiar, Krissia Zawadzki, Helena Bragan\c{c}a
items.summary: We investigate how equilibrium quantum phase transitions manifest themselves in small systems driven out of equilibrium by quantum quenches. We consider linear ramps of the anisotropy in spin-1/2 and spin-1 XXZ chains, which host transitions of first, second, and infinite (Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless, BKT) order. We consider system sizes available in current quantum simulators and investigate how the order of the transition, the symmetries, and the ramp duration affect the decomposition of the time-evolved state into the instantaneous eigenbasis. The order of the transition determines the dynamics: across the BKT transition, moderately slow ramps already keep the system close to its ground state, corresponding to an adiabatic evolution, whereas for the second-order Haldane-N\'eel transition a ramp roughly three times slower is required to reach the same regime. Across the first-order transition, since the dynamics conserves the magnetization of the initial state, we observe the formation of ferromagnetic domains, separated by a single domain wall for slow ramps and by multiple walls for faster ones. Interestingly, shortly after the transition, the state evolves as a coherent beating between domain-wall states, a behavior captured by the recently proposed quantum-state texture.

items.title: Adaptive nonorthogonal atomic orbitals refine charge transfer and bonding descriptors
authors: Emily Oliphant, Emmanouil Kioupakis, Wenhao Sun
items.summary: First-principles calculations implicitly encode bonding and charge transfer, but converting periodic electronic structure into interpretable and transferable descriptors remains challenging. Recently, we introduced Crystal Orbital Guided Iteration To atomic-Orbitals (COGITO), a tool for mapping plane-wave DFT back to an interpretable, minimal basis of adaptive atomic orbitals. Here, we show how the high-dimensional bonding information from COGITO can be reduced into chemically useful descriptors of covalent bonding, charge transfer, and crystal-dependent atomic chemistry without collapsing the real-space origin of the interactions. Compared to methods that use static or orthogonal orbital bases, COGITO descriptors of short- and long-range bonding show more stability and a better ability to distinguish between ionic, covalent, and metallic bonding regimes. Lastly, COGITO reliably decomposes band dispersion into range-resolved contributions, allowing us to verify and add to the orbital origins of silicon's low-symmetry conduction band minimum. Overall, the adaptive COGITO-based descriptors encode electronic structure, offering a well-structured route to expose the orbital interactions and charge transfer responsible for electronic properties.

items.title: Flat-band driven bipolar anomalous Nernst effect towards volt-scale transverse thermoelectric conversion
authors: Haofu Wen, Xiaodong Guo, Xiaokang Xu, Peng Di, Xuebiao Ji, Ruoqi Wang, Shijun Yuan, Kunquan Hong, Qionghua Zhou, Qian Chen, Taishi Chen, Jinlan Wang
items.summary: Unipolar anomalous Nernst thermopiles are critically plagued by metallic interconnects, which induce heavy Joule dissipation and compromise the module's packing density, ultimately capping voltage generation. Here, we circumvent these limitations by establishing an intrinsic bipolar anomalous Nernst effect (BANE) paradigm, enabling seamless series integration analogous to Seebeck n-p pairs without passive metallic bridges. Focusing on flat-band topological systems, through machine learning assisted screening across multiple target properties, we identified 249 BANE materials, exhibiting near-room-temperature polarity switching. Guided by this predictive framework, we experimentally realized this phenomenon in single crystals of the Weyl ferromagnet, Co$_2$TiGe. Strikingly, while its intrinsic anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC) remains rigorously temperature-invariant up to the Curie temperature, the anomalous Nernst signal undergoes a sharp polarity inversion across $T \approx 225$ K. First-principles calculations attribute this behavior to the interplay between flat bands and Weyl nodes, where thermal depopulation shifts the chemical potential across the band edge, inverting the sign of $\partial \sigma_{xy} / \partial \epsilon$ via the Mott relation. This work opens an avenue toward compact, monolithic transverse thermopiles capable of volt-scale generation free from interfacial parasitic dissipation.

items.title: Emergence of Anisotropic Defect Networks in Shocked Diamond
authors: Zipeng Xu, Kento Katagiri, Tatiana Pikuz, Wanghui Li, Anirudh Hari, Dorian P. Luccioni, Sophie E. Parsons, Yuichi Inubushi, Kohei Miyanishi, Hirotaka Nakamura, Tadashi Togashi, Makina Yabashi, Toshinori Yabuuchi, Norimasa Ozaki, Leora E. Dresselhaus-Marais
items.summary: Predicting failure after shock loading requires understanding how the structures created during compression evolve as the material unloads. In diamond, both crystal plasticity and localized amorphization have been reported to accommodate shock-induced shear. However, it remains unresolved how the resulting defect structures organize in three dimensions during compression and how this organization influences where tensile damage localizes during release. Here we couple phase-contrast-enhanced radiography at an X-ray free-electron laser with simulations to address this question in single-crystal diamond. By combining radiographs at multiple pump-probe delays with hydrodynamic calculations, we show that linear features first become visible behind the plastic wavefront while material near the front remains highly compressed. By rotating the viewing direction about the shock axis, we find that the projected feature angles favor finite $\{111\}$ sheets elongated along in-plane directions close to $\langle112\rangle$. Molecular dynamics simulations show that an interconnected network of amorphous bands and stacking faults forms during compression, preferentially on $\{111\}$ variants with larger in-plane shear traction. Projections of this network qualitatively reproduce the observed loss of feature visibility with rotation. During simulated release, tension opens local cracks within these pre-existing amorphous bands. These results support a pathway in which the crystallographically organized defect network formed during compression provides preferred sites for tensile damage during release. This pathway may also operate in other strongly covalent solids.

items.title: SPARC: Evidence-guided adaptive model composition for materials discovery
authors: Sissi Feng, Yuchen Han, Runze Zhang, Jiaru Bai, Brandon Sutherland, Ali Shayesteh Zeraati, Jason Hattrick-Simpers, Varinia Bernales, Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik, Yang Bai
items.summary: Closed-loop experimentation requires more than selecting the next experiment. It must also determine which existing measurements and model-derived relationships are sufficiently supported to influence that decision. Here we introduce SPARC (Sparse Predictive Aggregation of Regression Components), a framework that continually revises this support as experimental evidence accumulates. Competing model families are evaluated through out-of-fold predictions, so that each model is tested on observations not used in its corresponding fit. Sparse posterior composition assigns model influence according to predictive contributions supported by the out-of-fold evidence, retaining complementary contributions from several model families. Candidate-dependent predictive dispersion and residual variability define trust, which modulates exploration alongside the predicted response. Independent diagnostics also prioritize existing measurements for prospective verification, with model-derived trust reported alongside them. Across eight published materials datasets, SPARC achieved higher $R^2$ than the corresponding literature-reported values in six, with relative gains of up to 77% without the density-functional-theory- or experiment-derived descriptors used by several published pipelines. In an automated alkaline oxygen-evolution-reaction campaign, 8 of 11 SPARC-selected experiments reached overpotentials below 300 mV, with a best value of 242 mV, compared with 18 of 125 initial experiments. Measurements prioritized for verification before repetition subsequently deviated by 76 mV on average, compared with 27 mV for matched controls. SPARC therefore turns experimental evidence into a basis for revising model influence, directing exploration and identifying measurements that warrant verification.

items.title: Quasi-particle sector hybridization and the onset of chaos in spin ladders
items.summary: How quasiparticle numbers influence the emergence of quantum chaos is a fundamental question in interacting many-body systems. We investigate this interplay in a spin-$1/2$ XXZ ladder, where the strong-rung regime supports an approximate organization of many-body eigenstates into quasi-particle(triplon) number sectors. Using spectral statistics, triplon-based observables, and von Neumann entanglement entropy, we characterize the microscopic hybridization of triplon-number sectors as the leg coupling increases. We find that the crossover toward Gaussian orthogonal ensemble statistics shifts to weaker couplings with increasing system size, whereas the characteristic crossover scale associated with triplon-sector hybridization exhibits a much weaker size dependence. Furthermore, eigenstate-to-eigenstate fluctuations exhibit scaling consistent with the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis even while remnants of the strong-rung structure persist, suggesting that spectral chaos does not necessarily require complete sector hybridization.

items.title: Interplay of interfacial energetics and selective Ni segregation in the morphology of co-precipitates in low-alloy steels
authors: Jia-Hong Ke, Anshul Kamboj, Mukesh Bachhav
items.summary: Coupled precipitation and interfacial segregation in low-alloy steels change precipitate stability and morphology, which influence strengthening and embrittlement. Cu-rich precipitates (CRPs) and Mn-Ni-Si-rich precipitates (MNSPs) frequently form core-shell or appendage morphologies, but the interfacial energetics controlling this change are not well quantified. We combine a density-functional-theory-trained cluster expansion with lattice Monte Carlo simulations to evaluate the Fe/CRP, Fe/MNSP and Cu/MNSP interfaces within one Hamiltonian. The three coefficients based on excess internal energy follow gamma_Cu/MNSP < gamma_Fe/CRP <~ gamma_Fe/MNSP and give a positive work of adhesion and a negative spreading parameter, consistent with favorable Mn-Ni-Si attachment to a CRP and partial coverage. Only Ni segregates to the Fe/CRP boundary. Mn and Si segregate weakly on their own but become more enriched when Ni is present and co-segregate with Ni at the boundary. Ni forms an interfacial layer about one monolayer thick with an excess of 7.4-9.6 atoms/nm^2, develops B2-like local order and shows an energy reduction that increases with Ni coverage. At 1 at.% matrix Ni, a Gibbs adsorption analysis gives a Fe/CRP free-energy reduction of about 0.15 J/m^2. These interface coefficients and segregation trends connect segregation, interface energy and co-precipitation and support compositional optimization in low-alloy steels.

items.title: Spontaneous Chiral Superradiance of a Spin-1 Condensate in a Ring Cavity
authors: Jingjun You, Haoran Jia, Xinyu Feng, Zhenhua Yu, Su Yi, Yuangang Deng
items.summary: We investigate superradiant phase transitions in a spin-$1$ Bose-Einstein condensate coupled to a ring cavity, where two symmetry-related Raman processes couple the atomic spin states to counterpropagating cavity modes. Above the superradiant threshold, we find that the symmetry between the two Raman channels is spontaneously broken, giving rise to a chiral superradiant (CSR) phase. Despite the exchange symmetry of the Hamiltonian, the CSR state spontaneously selects one of the two propagation directions, with one cavity mode becoming macroscopically occupied while its counterpropagating partner remains dark. Spin-dependent collisions further reshape the superradiant phase diagram by selectively shifting the boundaries between the chiral and symmetric superradiant phases, a feature intrinsic to the multicomponent spin-$1$ manifold. For sufficiently negative spin-dependent interactions, the interaction-induced modification of the atomic level structure gives rise to a reversed plane-wave phase characterized by an inverted internal-state occupation. These results identify spontaneous selection between symmetry-related superradiant channels as a mechanism for generating chirality in many-body cavity QED and demonstrate how spin-dependent collisions control the resulting superradiant phase structure.

items.title: Exact mobility edges in high-dimensional quasiperiodic networks
authors: Jia-Hui Zhang, Shan-Zhong Li, Zhi Li
items.summary: Inspired by the one-dimensional hidden self-duality [Phys. Rev. Lett. 134, 246301 (2025)], we establish a generalized theoretical framework for a specific class of high-dimensional quasiperiodic network models. Specifically, as long as the periodic network acts as bond-decorating links and the quasiperiodic potentials are spatially separable, the system can be mapped onto an effective high-dimensional generalized Aubry-Andr\'e equation by integrating out the periodic sites. This mapping restores the hidden self-duality symmetry in these complex models, thereby yielding exact mobility edges. Taking two-dimensional and three-dimensional models as examples, we demonstrate the consistency between the theoretical prediction and the numerical results. This paper establishes a clear paradigm for mapping high-dimensional quasiperiodic networks to high-dimensional Aubry-Andr\'e models, providing a systematic pathway for the construction and exploration of the exact mobility edge in high-dimensional systems.

items.title: A mesoscale damage model for void nucleation and growth in shock loaded microstructure informed by computer vision
items.summary: Spallation in ductile materials under high strain rates occurs through the process of void nucleation, growth, and coalescence. Void nucleation is known to depend on factors ranging from microstructural to stress state. The criteria for void nucleation in damage models are stochastic, and microstructural awareness is often neglected. Recently, it was shown that nucleation propensity can be estimated using computer vision. In the present work, this is integrated with a continuum damage model framework for comprehensive simulation of spallation in tantalum under plate impact. Void nucleation probability is governed by a susceptibility field, predicted from grain orientations and grain boundary (GB) energy, with a mechanical barrier set by the local maximum principal stress. This is coupled to a crystal plasticity model within a Lagrangian shock simulation, with microstructure selectively resolved to reduce computational cost. The model is calibrated at a flyer velocity of 196 m/s, where the simulated free surface velocity (FSV) matches experimental measurements of shock arrival, peak state, release and the pullback signal measured in flyer impact experiments, with some deviations confined to the late time ringing. With no further parameter changes, the model transfers to a 214 m/s case and accurately reproduces the FSV. To demonstrate the microstructure-awareness of the nucleation model, a selection of synthetic microstructures is presented for comparison. In the resolved microstructure, voids nucleate predominantly (though not exclusively) at GBs and triple junctions. It is shown that the FSV differs significantly based on the incorporated microstructure, yielding the correct FSV prediction only in the case of representative microstructures.

items.title: Higher-order statistical structure in perfume item combinations beyond a pairwise maximum-entropy model
items.summary: We find that deviations from a pairwise maximum-entropy model in perfume item combinations are organized around particular shared item pairs. We analyze 1,979 perfumes using 50 binary variables representing the most frequently listed items. Although the pairwise model approximately reproduces the distribution of the number of listed items per perfume, the observed three-item marginal distributions exhibit deviations exceeding those obtained from synthetic datasets subjected to the same model-refitting procedure. Strongly deviating triplets are concentrated around shared item pairs, and this concentration cannot be explained by the participation frequencies of individual items alone. We then introduce three-body couplings for 50 selected triplets and reoptimize all model parameters. The sum of squared standardized residuals over the remaining 19,550 triplets decreases by 5.44\%, with substantially larger reductions for triplets sharing an item pair with selected triplets. Furthermore, a static linear-response calculation accounting for the readjustment of lower-order parameters approximately reproduces the resulting changes in predicted co-occurrence frequencies, with a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.850. These results reveal the organization of higher-order statistical dependencies and characterize how selected three-body couplings affect predictions throughout the system.

items.title: Chiral-phonon-mediated spin current injection into an Ising superconductor
authors: Jiayan Zhang, Gaoyang Li, Yanxia Xing
items.summary: We theoretically propose chiral-phonon-mediated spin current injection into an Ising superconductor in a chiral-insulator/Ising-superconductor heterostructure, where nonequilibrium phonons driven by a temperature gradient transfer their angular momentum to electron spins via interfacial phonon-spin conversion. Using the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism, we derive an expression for the injected spin current and show that it depends on the difference between the contributions from the two phonon branches with opposite circular polarizations. We further investigate the temperature dependence of the injected spin current density at different in-plane magnetic field strengths. In the superconducting state, the spin current density increases with temperature or in-plane magnetic field strength. In addition to the kink at the superconducting transition, a second kink appears below the transition temperature. The position of this kink is consistent with the onset of phonon-induced two-quasiparticle excitations as the superconducting gap decreases with increasing temperature. We further investigate the magnetic-field dependence of the kink temperature in a temperature--magnetic-field phase diagram.

items.title: Optical response of quantum metals
authors: Erik van Heumen, Martin Dressel, Simone Fratini
items.summary: Strongly interacting quantum systems display puzzling electrical transport properties whose interpretation remains controversial. Many theoretical and phenomenological analyses assume that the complex behaviour observed in such `quantum materials' originates either from quasi-particles dressed with an anomalous electron self-energy or from collective excitations associated with hydrodynamic flow. Despite their distinctly different starting points, the underlying assumption is that dissipation of electrical current arises from the relaxation of the total momentum of charge carriers. This classical description breaks down in the absence of long-lived charge carriers. In such strange metals dissipation seems to be governed by the rate at which equilibrium is thermally restored, and it has been suggested that this constitutes an upper bound, known as the `Planckian limit'. Here we show that in this quantum regime a description of the conductivity in terms of relaxation rates no longer suffices: strange metal transport is carried instead by fast-decaying current fluctuations, which together with quantum detailed balance give rise to the widely observed Planckian dissipation. The distinction between classical and quantum metals becomes transparent when experimental data is analysed in terms of the current-current correlation function instead of the optical conductivity. When applied to the cuprate superconductors, such analysis uncovers that the strange metal response is present at all doping levels, and that a second, classical component develops above optimal doping. This simple, but powerful, approach further highlights essential features associated with superconductivity, (pseudo-)gaps, provides fresh insight in the properties of metals, and identifies key areas where progress in our theoretical understanding is needed.

items.title: Fragmentation in Non-Hermitian Many-Body Systems
items.summary: In non-Hermitian (NH) fermionic chains with spatially random imaginary gauge fields, single-particle eigenstates exhibit erratic NH skin localization with strongly fluctuating, subexponential decay, distinct from both conventional skin accumulation and Anderson localization. At finite filling, Pauli exclusion suppresses macroscopic accumulation and instead leads to fragmentation of the particle density, in sharp contrast to Hermitian disordered systems. Using exact free-fermion methods, we show that the density organizes into disconnected regions of high and low occupancy, forming spatially separated Fermi domains whose number $N_{\mathrm{FS}}$ scales subextensively with system size $L$. Remarkably, fragmentation is not only an equilibrium property but also emerges dynamically in the NH evolution, unlike in Hermitian systems where such structures are not dynamically selected. This behavior admits a Coulomb-gas description in a stochastic potential, establishing a direct link between erratic NH skin localization and real-space fragmentation of many-body states.

items.title: Thermal-energy relaxation in chiral quantum Hall edge mode
items.summary: We study the nonequilibrium state generated by a real Ohmic contact (ROC) in the charge-fractionalization regime. We then investigate its thermal-energy relaxation along a quantum Hall edge mediated by a fictitious Ohmic contact (FOC) with large capacitance and perfect coupling to the edge. For cold Ohmic contacts, the electron distribution function and current noise are fully described by their equilibrium forms and the corresponding Fermi-Dirac distribution. In contrast, in the case of hot Ohmic contacts, strong thermalization effects do not drive the outgoing state into complete equilibrium. Both the distribution function and the noise retain signatures of the initial nonequilibrium state and therefore cannot be characterized solely by the effective contact temperature, contrary to common assumptions.

items.title: Inelastic confinement-induced resonances in multiwell potentials
items.summary: Recently, resonance features associated with multiwell effects have been reported in a fascinating experiment conducted with an ultracold-atom quantum simulator [Y. K. Lee, H. Lin, and W. Ketterle, Phys. Rev. Lett. 131, 213001 (2023)]. The results were explained as a consequence of superexchange, which determines the spin dynamics in a singly-occupied Mott insulator, by allowing for the virtual population of two particles on the same site. In this work, a complementary interpretation of the resonance features is provided based on inelastic confinement-induced resonances, manifested as avoided crossings in the two-particle spectrum, showing excellent agreement with the experimental results. The comparison of the results of the single- and double-well descriptions of the optical trapping potential confirms the multiwell origin of the experimental features. However, the double-well model is already shown to be sufficient for providing an explanation of the apparent symmetry violation that occurs within single-well models. Furthermore, certain limitations of the harmonic approximation are discussed.

items.title: Knitting the Ising Transition: Statistical Physics as a Tool for Stochastic Knit Design
authors: Gabrielle Chang, Kafumi Akaho, Tomohiko G. Sano, Samuel Poincloux
items.summary: Textile designs are typically based on biperiodic, deterministic patterns. However, hand and machine manufacturing are not restricted to periodic patterns. Instead, the entanglement topology can be chosen for each base unit cell of the textile. Non-deterministic processes, such as stochastic realisations of physical systems, can then serve as design tools for creating original patterns. In this Proceedings, we present a proof of concept for stochastic design by generating knitted fabrics from Ising model spin patterns. We leverage the binary analogy between knit/purl stitches and up/down spins to produce fabrics that directly represent spin realisations at different temperatures. Ising patterns then play the role of topological instructions to arrange the entanglements in the fabric. This proof of concept paves the way for novel stochastic designs of fabrics whose properties are directly controlled by the statistical characteristics of an underlying physical process.

items.title: When the Boundary Changes the Bulk: Topological Edge Modes in Dynamical Quantum Phase Transitions
items.summary: For dynamical quantum phase transitions (DQPTs) in open chains it has been noted that the boundary can change the bulk: in time windows bounded by DQPTs, exponentially localized edge modes of the Loschmidt matrix produce a finite change in the intensive return rate. These modes have been attributed to topological properties of the initial and final Hamiltonians. Here we show that it is not the topology of the Hamiltonians but rather that of the non-Hermitian Loschmidt matrix which protects these edge modes. In particular, we show that topological edge modes can exist in class A, where both Hamiltonians are topologically trivial. For classes A, BDI, and AIII we show that these modes are protected by $\mathbb{Z}$ indices of a Toeplitz operator and that K-splitting theorems provide a precise bulk-boundary correspondence. In class D, they are protected instead by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ index that records whether the quench has flipped the fermion parity at the edge. The bulk invariant for class D can be formulated either as a ratio of the Loschmidt amplitudes for periodic and anti-periodic boundary conditions or as a winding number that counts phase vortices in momentum and time. We discuss examples and provide numerical data for all four topological classes.

items.title: Tunable topological droplets on supercoiled DNA under tension
authors: Enrico Skoruppa, Prithwidip Saha, Jan Brugu\'es, Jan Lipfert, Davide Marenduzzo, Helmut Schiessel
items.summary: DNA--protein co-condensation is an important regulatory mechanism for gene expression and repair. For straight DNA under constant stretching forces, co-condensation is ``all-or-nothing'': above a critical force, condensates are prevented from nucleating, while below it the entire molecule collapses into a droplet. Here we show by coarse-grained simulations and analytic theory that DNA supercoiling mechanically differentiates the condensation substrate: DNA plectonemes constitute force-insulated pockets on which condensates can nucleate even above the critical force. The size of the resulting droplets is tunable through the applied force and linking number. Surface tension drives the coarsening of multiple plectoneme-associated condensates into a single topological droplet. Magnetic tweezers experiments with spermine reproduce both the force-dependent collapse and the supercoiling-dependent condensation.

items.title: Exploring Energy Landscapes for Functional Materials: Ga vacancies in $\beta$-Ga$_{2}$O$_{3}$
authors: Soon Woo Park, Philipp Pracht, Se\'an R. Kavanagh, David J. Wales
items.summary: Energy landscape exploration requires extensive energy and force evaluations, making efficient access to interatomic potentials an important practical challenge. We present a persistent socket interface that connects the landscape exploration tools in the GMIN, OPTIM, and PATHSAMPLE programs to potentials available through the Atomic Simulation Environment (ASE). The persistent design keeps both the calculator and socket connection active throughout the search, avoiding repeated initialisation. We apply this framework to understand and predict the properties of Ga vacancies in $\beta$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ using two NequIP-based potentials, and construct kinetic transition networks describing complex vacancy configurations and migration pathways. Temperature-dependent analysis of the dominant paths reveals how the most probable migration sequence can change, with the mechanism governed by global properties of the network, rather than simply the highest energy barrier. Visualisation, mean first-passage times, and heat capacities enable us to connect the organisation of the landscape to relaxation time scales and thermodynamic observables. The interface extends energy landscape methods to ASE-compatible atomistic models, providing a general framework for combining global optimisation, transition state searches, kinetic network analysis, and thermodynamic characterisation with recent developments in machine-learned interatomic potentials.

items.title: Porosification of the dielectric layer in alternating-current electroluminescence devices enables high-resolution tactile imaging
authors: Mingwei Gu, Licheng Li, Zeyuan Zhou, Ying Yang, Zixiang Nie, Xingyu Ma, Junshuai Chen, Lin Zheng, Jinhui Gu, Jia-Sen Xie, Ziling Wei, Mengxing Huang, Jin Ge
items.summary: Vision-based tactile sensing enables high-resolution contact perception, yet bulky optical architectures consume valuable space and constrain the functional design of dexterous robotic hands. Here we introduce a self-emissive tactile imaging strategy based on alternating-current electroluminescence (ACEL) devices, in which a compressible porous dielectric encodes contact pressure into spatial emission patterns without external illumination or discrete sensing pixels. We identify a nonlinear capacitance-dependent emission window that provides a basis for tunable pressure-to-light conversion. Pore-size engineering further suppresses local emission deficiencies, reducing spatial intensity variation by nearly ninefold and enabling faithful imaging of contact features down to 100 {\mu}m. The continuous electroluminescent interface also reproduces complex contact patterns without computational reconstruction of electrical fields. Direct lamination of the ACEL device onto a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) image sensor is expected to enable compact contact imaging in an assembly less than 5 mm thick, substantially thinner than conventional vision-based tactile sensors. This approach could reduce the space required for high-resolution tactile imaging, offering greater design freedom for dexterous robotic hands.

items.title: Finite-size scaling of $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking decoupled from thermodynamic criticality in a complex-conjugate Ising model
authors: Yihan Wang, Yuting Wang, Lihui Sun, Qionglin Dai, Haihong Li, Lufeng Zhang, Yuhai Liu
items.summary: We study a two-dimensional anisotropic Ising model with complex-conjugate couplings. Analytic continuation of the exact anisotropic Ising critical condition yields a candidate thermodynamic critical line, which is independently supported by finite-size scaling confirming the two-dimensional Ising universality class. Exact diagonalization of the transfer matrix and finite-size extrapolation reveal that the spectrum becomes complex, defining a separate $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry-breaking boundary in the thermodynamic limit. We find $K_{\rm PT}<K_c$ throughout the parameter range studied, leaving an intermediate regime with a complex spectrum while the system remains thermodynamically disordered. The spatial correlations remain short-ranged at $K_{\rm PT}$, in contrast to the critical correlations at $K_c$, directly distinguishing the spectral transition from thermodynamic criticality. The complex-conjugate anisotropy modifies the finite-size free-energy amplitude, and accounting for the corresponding anisotropy factor recovers the Ising central charge $c=1/2$. These results demonstrate that spectral $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetry breaking can occur without thermodynamic criticality, establishing a decoupling between spectral and thermodynamic transitions in a two-dimensional non-Hermitian statistical system.

items.title: Universal Analytical Description of Magnetoexcitons in Two-Dimensional Semiconducting Materials
authors: Dang-Khoa D. Le, Dai-Nam Le, Ngoc-Loan Phan, Van-Hoang Le
items.summary: Matching the Coulomb and logarithmic limits of the Rytova--Keldysh model gives a universal zero-field spectrum for monolayer exciton $s$ states, $E_n\simeq-\mathrm{Ry}^*/[n-1/2+f_n(\xi)]^2$, where $\xi$ is the screening parameter. Analytical radii determine diamagnetic coefficients and the magnetic crossover scale. Zero-field deviations peak near $1\%$ across the full screening range $0\leq\xi\leq100$. For the sampled hBN-encapsulated monolayers, magnetoexciton energies agree with numerical spectra to sub-meV rms up to $100\T$ and capture the measured orbital shifts. Shared parameters link optical and magneto-optical spectra.

items.title: Ultrastrong coupling between magnetoplasmons and higher cyclotron-resonance harmonics induced by spatially inhomogeneous electromagnetic fields in two-dimensional electron systems
authors: Kazuyuki Kuroyama, Shimpei Nakamura, Motoaki Bamba
items.summary: Finite-wave-vector electromagnetic fields provide a route to accessing nonlocal collective dynamics in two-dimensional electron systems. Here, we theoretically investigate the magnetoplasmon response of a two-dimensional electron system subjected to a spatially nonuniform electromagnetic field in a perpendicular magnetic field. By combining Maxwell's equations with the Kubo formula, we derive the nonlocal magnetoconductivity tensor and obtain the self-consistent dispersion relation for collective modes. We show that a finite in-plane wave vector enables higher-order cyclotron transitions, allowing higher harmonics of the cyclotron resonance to contribute to the nonlocal conductivity. These harmonics hybridize with the magnetoplasmon mode, producing avoided crossings in the collective-mode spectrum characteristic of Bernstein modes. To quantify this hybridization, we establish a correspondence between the Maxwell-Kubo dispersion relation and a Hopfield-type Hamiltonian and derive an analytical expression for the effective coupling strength between the magnetoplasmon and the n-th cyclotron-resonance harmonic. Our analysis reveals that the normalized coupling strength exhibits a nonmonotonic dependence on the in-plane wavelength, reaching a maximum that becomes nearly independent of electron density in the high-density regime. These results establish a quantitative connection between nonlocal magnetoconductivity, Bernstein-mode physics, and effective collective-mode coupling, providing design guidelines for realizing ultrastrong coupling in terahertz magnetoplasmonic systems.

items.title: Critical corner angles and defect exchange in confined nematics with splay-bend anisotropy
items.summary: In confined nematics, the director turning imposed by the walls is absorbed by defects, and we show that the corners exchange these defects with the liquid. A tangentially anchored corner of opening angle $\omega$ takes one of several types, labelled by the number $m$ of half-turns of the director relative to the radius; neighbouring types differ by a bound defect of index $\pm\frac12$, and logarithmic energies decide when the corner sheds or absorbs it. For equal elastic constants the critical angles are $72^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $216^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, with windows of bistability between them, explaining the hidden defect near $72^\circ$ vertices and selecting the equilibria of polygons and discs. We introduce unequal splay and bend constants through the cubic invariant $Q_{lk}\,\partial_lQ_{ij}\,\partial_kQ_{ij}$ in reduced Landau--de Gennes theory; bounding the order by its bulk value makes the problem well posed, without further elastic terms, whenever both Frank constants are positive. At first order only the splay corner feels the anisotropy; other corner and defect energies are even in it and follow exactly by quadrature. The anisotropy moves the angle above which a splay corner sheds a $+\frac12$ defect from $104^\circ$ to $136^\circ$ as $K_3/K_1$ rises from $0.54$ to $1.86$, and so predicts which polygons prefer splay corners and which interior defects. Finite-element computations for polygons of three to eight sides and the disc confirm this: the exchange occurs within the predicted range by migration of $+\frac12$ defects into the corners, near which states with zero, one and two splay corners are nearly degenerate.

items.title: A Universal Algebraic Construction of Hilbert-Space Fragmentation
items.summary: We present a mechanism for obtaining Hilbert-space fragmentation from arbitrary quantum lattice Hamiltonians acting on finite-dimensional local spaces. We first express the Hamiltonian in an algebraic form using supersymmetry (SUSY) and parasupersymmetry (paraSUSY) generators. Enlarging their representations defines a lifting procedure, which we study in two forms, site-wise and bond-wise lifting. Site-wise lifting introduces immobile zero modes that generate exponentially many invariant sectors while retaining the original dynamics in the fully active sector. We determine the sector structure and establish strong fragmentation for uniform lifts at fixed intermediate zero-mode density. For nearest-neighbor chains, correlation functions reveal restricted propagation and, in the mixed-field example, persistent local memory. Bond-wise lifting produces mobile conserved strings, pair-flip dynamics and fluctuating dimers, and extends to fragmented unitary circuits. Different representations and embeddings realize different fragmentation mechanisms. Some of the fragmented models obtained by this method include lifted permutation and Ising spin chains, a lifted toric code, the \(XXC\) families of spin chains, and fragmented extensions derived from the integrable \(H_{1,11}\) and \(H_{1,3}\) seed densities. The last two models are derived from Hietarinta's classification of constant $4\times 4$ Yang-Baxter solutions.

items.title: Bright-Dark State Interplay Governs Vibronic Decoherence in Molecular Aggregates
authors: Sreeja Loho Choudhury, Abhradeep Sarkar, Raja Ghosh
items.summary: In this study, we establish a spectroscopy-driven framework that connects optically bright vibronic eigenstates to their subsequent decoherence dynamics in excitonic molecular aggregates. Combining the Multiparticle Holstein Formalism with explicit system--bath interactions, we demonstrate that relaxation-induced purity loss is governed by three interconnected factors: (i) the bath spectral window, which determines the accessibility of intra- and interband relaxation pathways; (ii) the local network of dark vibronic states surrounding the optically prepared bright state; and (iii) the energetic placement of the bright state, which controls downhill relaxation. Remarkably, states with different excitation energies exhibit nearly identical purity dynamics when their local relaxation networks are similar. The resulting H--J asymmetry further reveals the importance of energetic directionality. These findings establish a reliable connection between optical spectroscopy, vibronic band structure, and state-selective loss in purity.

items.title: Geodesics and a Hubble Relation in Nonstationary Thermodynamic Geometry
items.summary: Thermodynamic geometry offers a versatile lens from equilibrium to nonequilibrium, yet typically assumes a stationary metric. Here we study nonstationary thermodynamic geometry, where the metric evolves even at fixed control parameters. The resulting temporal connection generalizes the geodesic equation and redistributes dissipation along optimal control paths. We further establish a thermodynamic Hubble relation that distinguishes relaxation toward equilibrium from geometric expansion or contraction. Brownian examples demonstrate that externally modulated friction can reduce minimum dissipation, while heat exchange with a finite reservoir can induce geometric contraction and Mpemba-type relaxation. Our framework lays a geometric foundation for understanding complex evolving nonequilibrium systems.

items.title: A Neural Density Functional for Spatial Structure and Orientational Ordering in Two-Dimensional Lattice Hard Rods
authors: Paul Bitzer, Jens Weimar, Martin Oettel
items.summary: We study spatial structure and orientational ordering of horizontal and vertical hard rods on a two-dimensional square lattice using neural classical density functional theory. We construct two convolutional architectures that exploit the symmetry relating the rod orientations: a direct-$c^{(1)}$ network (learning the map between the first functional derivative of the excess free energy and the inhomogeneous density, $c^{(1)} \leftrightarrow \rho$) and a $\Phi$-network (learning directly the map between free energy and density, $F_\text{ex} \leftrightarrow \rho$). Both networks use exactly the same inhomogeneous grand-canonical Monte Carlo density profiles and one-body direct correlation targets. Both neural representations substantially improve the predicted density profiles relative to the Lafuente--Cuesta lattice functional. The resulting free energy landscapes, however, differ between the two representations. Furthermore for the direct-$c^{(1)}$ network the integration along different density paths produces different free energies. As a result, the transition to nematic ordering for rods with aspect ratio 8 is strongly first order for the direct-$c^{(1)}$ network while only weakly discontinuous for the $\Phi$-network. The latter is a reasonable approximation to the continuous transition found in simulations, demonstrating that subtle entropic free energy differences are accessible in neural cDFT.

items.title: Tracking gas-solid hydration kinetics by non-contact in situ transflection micro-FTIR spectroscopy
authors: Kunihiko Shizume, Hidetoshi Miyazaki, Yasushi Hamanaka
items.summary: Gas--solid reaction kinetics is important in applications such as thermochemical heat storage (TCHS), but experimental evaluation remains a bottleneck in materials development. This study evaluates non-contact \textit{in situ} transflection micro-Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy for tracking hydration reactions between water vapor and inorganic solids. Powder layers of La$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$, CaSO$_4$, and CaO, exhibiting different hydration mechanisms and kinetics, were deposited on an Au-coated glass substrate and exposed to humidified N$_2$. Evolution of water- and hydroxyl-related IR absorption band areas was compared with thermogravimetry (TG)-derived hydration numbers. The FTIR band-area profiles were broadly consistent with the TG-derived hydration trends, showing close agreement for La$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ and CaSO$_4$. For CaO, some differences were observed between the FTIR and TG results, possibly because CaO is sensitive to differences in gas-phase conditions, particularly the initial increase in humidity, between the two measurements. The spectra distinguished molecular-water uptake in La$_2$(SO$_4$)$_3$ and CaSO$_4$ from hydroxide formation in CaO. They also detected carbonate formation during CaO hydration. Thus, \textit{in situ} time-resolved FTIR separately monitored individual chemical reactions, whereas TG recorded only their combined effect on the sample mass. These results demonstrate the potential of transflection micro-FTIR for chemically selective monitoring of gas--solid reactions in small localized samples.

items.title: Current-driven chiral RKKY interaction in altermagnets
items.summary: The Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya (DM) interaction between magnetic moments usually requires spin--orbit coupling and broken inversion symmetry. We show that in a spin-split metal without spin--orbit coupling a charge current generates a DM interaction between localized spins. Using Keldysh Green's functions (GFs) with a drifting Fermi sea, we compute the Ruderman--Kittel--Kasuya--Yosida (RKKY) interaction between two magnetic impurities in a two-dimensional $d$-wave altermagnet with an additional exchange splitting. To linear order in the current, the correction is a Fermi-surface term, and all its components are obtained in closed form in terms of Bessel functions, valid for arbitrary values of the two independent spin splittings, $\beta$ and $J_\perp$. The induced DM vector points along the spin-quantization axis, which in the present model is the out-of-plane direction $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$. At long distance it decays as $1/R$, one power more slowly than the equilibrium coupling. In the altermagnet it vanishes for bonds along the nodal directions, where the two spin bands are degenerate, and, for a diagonal current, has opposite signs on bonds along the two crystal axes. This $d$-wave signature reverses with the N\'eel vector and with the current, and distinguishes the altermagnet from a ferromagnet. The current also generates symmetric couplings that are odd in the impurity separation. In low-density two-dimensional conductors, the DM coupling can reach a few percent of the equilibrium exchange.

items.title: Field-Effect Magnon Transistor
authors: Qian Song, Sergei Prokhorenko, Thomas Cleveland, Ashish Omar, Zhi Yao, Sajid Husain, Peter Meisenheimer, Bowen Hao, Ziye Zhu, Pushpendra Gupta, Shashank Ojha, Nicholas Reiterer, Maya Ramesh, Sergio Puebla, Darrell Schlom, Tong Zhou, Laurent Bellaiche, Lane W. Martin, Ramamoorthy Ramesh
items.summary: Antiferromagnetic magnons offer a promising platform for highspeed, energy-efficient information processing. Intrinsic odd-parity spin splitting in a cycloidal magnetic order offers a route to nonvanishing magnon transport in compensated magnets. Here, we propose a magnonic field-effect device (akin to a transistor) based on a ferroelectric antiferromagnet BiFeO3 in which a gate electric field reconfigures domain boundaries to amplify/modulate magnon transport. These boundaries switch the nonlocal inverse-spin-Hall response between low- and high-signal states, with a pronounced dependence on the direction of magnon propagation. Source-drain reversal, magnetic-field measurements, symmetry analysis, and first-principles calculations reveal nonreciprocal magnon transport associated with the reversal of spin angular momentum across the domain boundaries. Our results establish an electrically programmable, non-volatile magnon transistor.

items.title: Chiral Majorana Charge Kondo Criticality
items.summary: Unambiguous identification of chiral Majorana edge modes remains challenging because the transport signatures proposed for them can also arise from conventional mechanisms. Here we identify the chiral Majorana charge Kondo (CMCK) critical point as a more discriminating many-body route to detect chiral Majorana edge modes. This criticality arises in a charged island hosting a single chiral Majorana edge mode, where Majorana self-conjugacy locks normal and anomalous tunneling amplitudes, so that each physical lead provides two Kondo screening channels without fine tuning. Ordinary subgap states generically break this locking and drive the system toward conventional charge Kondo (CK) behavior. In the simplest two-terminal geometry, CMCK and conventional CK share the critical conductance $G^*=e^2/2h$, but their leading conductance corrections scale as $T^{1/3}$ and $T$, respectively. Their residual entropies also differ, as do the crossover exponents under gate detuning and contact asymmetry. For $N$ leads, CMCK conductance corrections scale as $T^{1/(N+1)}$, and for $N\geq3$ even the critical conductance differs from that of conventional CK with the same number of leads. These universal signatures are testable using established charge-Kondo measurement techniques.

items.title: Scaling laws in machine learning on non-ideal experimental data enable inverse design of radiative-cooling coatings
authors: Kunihiko Shizume, Jiawen Li, Yaerim Lee, Yuki Asano, Tuwei Liao, Koji Tsuda, Junichiro Shiomi
items.summary: Materials informatics increasingly targets multicomponent materials, yet experimental datasets inevitably contain non-ideal variations arising from imperfect uniformity and reproducibility in composition, coating formation, and measurement. Whether machine-learning prediction accuracy scales with amount of data under these conditions remains unclear. Here, we develop an automated platform that produced and optically characterized 11,520 radiative-cooling coatings spanning nine material and processing parameters. Forward and inverse neural networks, and a spectrum-conditioned diffusion model were trained on subsets of 10 to 10,000 samples. All models exhibited power-law scaling, with prediction errors decreasing with dataset size. Experimental inverse-design validation showed that larger datasets produced spectra closer to a broadband-emitter target. The diffusion model generated multiple candidate parameter sets, allowing selection among alternative solutions based on ease of fabrication, cost, and scalability. These results demonstrate predictable learning-curve scaling in non-ideal experimental data and provide a quantitative basis for estimating the benefit of additional experimental data, and thus the cost-effectiveness of materials-informatics.

items.title: State-space symmetry in Boolean network ensembles
items.summary: Studies of evolving Boolean network systems have found that Boolean functions cluster into equivalence classes with a characteristic frequency distribution - a pattern governed by the Zyklenzeiger symmetry group - but the dynamical origin of this symmetry has remained unexplained. Here we show that it is a consequence of a fundamental symmetry of Boolean network dynamics itself. A Boolean network consists of nodes that update according to Boolean functions of their regulatory inputs; its global dynamics is encoded in a state-space network. We identify the dynamical symmetry group of ensembles of Boolean networks that average over random interaction topologies: for networks with $N$ nodes, it is the $N$-dimensional hyperoctahedral group, generated by node-flips and node-label permutations. These transformations are admissible for every Boolean network regardless of topology; for random-topology ensembles, including all ensembles of fixed in-degree $K<N$, they constitute the complete symmetry group. We also show that input-label permutations constitute a hidden gauge freedom of the dynamics. The Zyklenzeiger symmetry of Boolean functions follows directly from the node-flips of the hyperoctahedral group together with this gauge freedom. Boolean networks related by the hyperoctahedral group have isomorphic state-space networks and form its orbits, and Burnside's lemma gives the number of these orbits for any fixed network topology. It provides a symmetry reduction of the analysis of Boolean network dynamics and explains why the Boolean functions of evolved networks fall into Zyklenzeiger classes, and why these classes split in finite networks.

items.title: Quadrupole Origin of the Orbital Hall Effect in an $sp^3$ Centrosymmetric Lattice: Robustness and Tunability under Disorder
authors: Kevin J. U. Vidarte, Henrique P. Veiga, Aur\'elien Manchon, Tatiana G. Rappoport
items.summary: We investigate how disorder affects orbital Hall transport in the centrosymmetric spinless $sp^3$ tight-binding model on a square lattice, widely used as a minimal model for the orbital Hall effect [1]. In the pristine system, the intrinsic orbital Hall response is related to the quadrupolar orbital texture generated by $s$-$p$ hybridization. Using the Kubo-Bastin formalism expanded in Chebyshev polynomials, we analyze the effect of vacancies, orbital-dependent Anderson on-site disorder, and selective $V_{sp\sigma}$-bond disorder on the orbital transport. For Anderson disorder and vacancies, the longitudinal charge conductivity decreases faster than the orbital Hall conductivity over the range studied, leading to an increase of the orbital Hall angle and, in the Anderson case, saturation at stronger disorder. Selective $V_{sp\sigma}$-bond disorder behaves differently: by modifying only the $s$-$p$ hybridization channel while leaving the remaining hopping network intact, it can produce a non-monotonic orbital Hall response and enhance the orbital Hall conductivity at intermediate dilution. Overall, our results show that the orbital Hall response remains sizable under vacancy and on-site disorder, while selective modification of the $s$-$p$ hybridization provides an additional route to tune the orbital Hall conductivity.

items.title: Energetics of Coherent Heterophase Interfaces: Separating Chemical and Strain Contributions
authors: Adolfo Salgado-Casanova, Jacob Pietryga, Yi Xia, Chris Wolverton
items.summary: Coherent interfacial energies govern the formation and evolution of multiphase microstructures, but their calculation is complicated by the elastic energy required to accommodate lattice mismatch. Here, we construct a high-throughput DFT database of 365 coherent FCC/FCC, BCC/BCC, and HCP/HCP interfaces involving 41 metallic elements and lattice mismatches of up to 25%. We use the supercell approach, consisting of constructing superlattices of different thicknesses to separate the coherency strain energy from the chemical contribution to the interfacial energy. We classify the results according to the long-range ordering tendency of each binary system and the sign of the calculated interfacial energy. Most phase-separating systems exhibit positive interfacial energies, whereas most compound-ordering systems exhibit negative values, reflecting favorable unlike-atom bonding. Exceptions show that the chemical preference at a particular interface need not coincide with bulk phase behavior: coherency strain can oppose ordering, and stable compounds can adopt structures distinct from the calculated superlattices. No clear correlation of interfacial energy with lattice mismatch is observed, whereas coherency strain energy increases with mismatch. For phase-separating systems, the lowest interfacial energies generally occur along the closest-packed orientations, while this trend is absent for ordering systems. Comparisons with reported interfacial energies and binary phase diagrams show qualitative consistency, although quantitative agreement varies with reference states, structural constraints, and temperature.
